title: Reading a blackwork chart
subtitle: Every cell is a thread intersection, every marked cell is one stitch
excerpt: A blackwork chart is a grid where each square represents one fabric thread intersection. Dark squares show where the needle travels. Once you understand the grid, any blackwork pattern becomes a set of simple navigation decisions.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776, counted embroidery chapter. Caulfeild and Saward, Dictionary of Needlework (1882), Holbein stitch entry.
aliases: reading a counted chart for blackwork

glossaryTerms.definition: Double-running stitch worked along a counted path so the thread looks identical on both sides of the fabric. The traditional outline stitch for reversible blackwork.
Fabric woven with the same number of threads per centimetre in both directions. Blackwork is counted over these even intersections.
Understanding that each grid square on a chart represents one stitch position on evenweave fabric, and navigating the grid to place stitches correctly.
A stitch worked by bringing the needle up one stitch length ahead, then inserting it back at the end of the previous stitch. Forms a solid line.

content.text: A blackwork chart is a grid where every square is one stitch position on your
evenweave
fabric.

The grid lines on the chart map directly to the thread intersections in your cloth. A filled square means a stitch sits there. An empty square means the fabric shows through. That is the whole system. Once you see the grid as a map of thread positions,
reading a counted chart
becomes straightforward navigation.
What the chart symbols mean

Traditional blackwork charts use a simple convention. Filled or marked squares are stitched; empty squares are unworked fabric. Because blackwork is almost always one colour of thread, most charts use a single fill style with no colour key needed.

Some charts show the direction of stitching with small arrows or draw the stitch path explicitly. Most fill-pattern charts leave the path implicit: you work horizontally across a row, then return along the same row to complete the second pass if working
Holbein stitch
How to count accurately
Find the centre of your chart. Most printed charts mark this with arrows on the margins. Count out from the centre to the first stitch in your row.
Find the centre of your fabric by folding it in half in each direction and creasing lightly. Mark with a loose thread if needed.
Use a highlighter strip or removable tape to mark your current row on the chart. Move it down each time you complete a row.
Count in groups of ten. Most charts show a heavier line or tick every ten squares to help you keep your place.
Check your stitch count at the end of each row by comparing the number of filled squares in that row on the chart with the number of stitches you see on the cloth.
Working from a repeating fill pattern

Many blackwork fills are small repeating units, typically four to ten squares wide. Once you stitch the first repeat correctly, subsequent repeats follow the same movement without re-reading the chart. Count the repeat size once, check it against your first stitched block, then work the rest from muscle memory and the occasional count-check.
Using
back stitch
versus Holbein stitch
The chart shows the finished appearance of the stitching, not the stitch path. Whether you work
back stitch
(single-pass, slightly raised) or
Holbein stitch
(double-running, reversible) is your choice. The chart looks the same either way. If reversibility matters, choose Holbein stitch and work the line twice.

items.symptom: Losing your place on the chart
items.cause: Working without a row marker so you are scanning the whole chart each time.
items.fix: Use a highlighter strip or a ruler to isolate the row you are working. Move it after each completed row.

items.symptom: The pattern shifts by one square
items.cause: Miscounting the repeat start point, especially on the second or third repeat.
items.fix: At the start of every new repeat, count back to the first stitch of the row and verify the spacing before continuing.

items.symptom: Thread looks different from the chart
items.cause: Working the stitches in the wrong direction so diagonal fills lean the wrong way.
items.fix: Check the chart key or stitch legend for the intended stitch direction. Diagonal stitches lean consistently in one direction across the design.
